The Three Disciplines of Ambidexterity

IDEATION, INCUBATION, AND SCALING

Everyone who’s ever taken a shower has had a good idea. It’s the person who gets out of the shower, dries off, and does something about it who makes a difference.

Nolan Bushnell, Silicon Valley pioneer and founder of Atari

T H E E X A M P L E S W E H AV E S H O W N I N C H A P T E R 5 suggest that, under the right circumstances and with the right leadership, companies can trans- form themselves and compete successfully in both existing and new markets and technologies. But as illustrated in Chapter 6 with the examples of IBM and Cisco, getting the balance only approximately right is no guarantee of success. The challenge is for leaders to design a process that can do three very separate things: repeatably generate new ideas, screen these to identify those that leverage a company’s assets and capabilities in ways that custom- ers value, and scale these ventures into profitable businesses. This requires mastery of three distinct innovation disciplines: (1) ideation, or the discovery and development of ideas for potential new businesses, (2) incubation, dur- ing which the new ideas are validated in the market, and (3) scaling, when existing assets and capabilities are reallocated to help the new venture grow.1

Successful ambidexterity requires all three of these—being good at only one or two is not sufficient. As we will see, companies that concentrate on ideation or incubation may generate and validate new ideas but, in the end,

can fail to scale them. For example, Cisco developed a successful process for ideation (the I-Zone) that produced more than twelve hundred ideas for potential $1 billion businesses. They also implemented a rigorous incuba- tion process (the vision-s trategy-e xecution approach) for validating these ideas. But they failed because they had no disciplined scaling methodology to ensure that the new ventures got the assets and capabilities necessary to grow. Several years ago, we met with a large Japanese electronics firm that had invested heavily in open innovation. They proudly noted that they had identified more than four hundred ideas for potential new products and businesses, but when pressed they acknowledged that only two of these had been commercialized. They were great at ideation but had no systematic way to validate or scale these ideas. In our experience, managers have too often concentrated on the first two of these disciplines and have neglected the third. In this chapter we illustrate how ambidexterity can be thought of in terms of these three disciplines—and how leaders can design each of these.

MEETING THE CHALLENGE OF DISRUPTION In the face of disruption, companies around the world have embraced a variety of efforts to drive innovation, including everything from setting up outposts in Silicon Valley, establishing corporate venture capital funds, embracing design thinking, adopting the lean start-u p methodology, and experimenting with open source innovation. For example, a survey of more than a hundred companies found that 92 percent claimed to have some in- volvement with start-u ps as a way to access new technology.2 IBM is reported to have more than sixteen hundred formally trained designers operating in forty-four studios.3 Companies such as Ford, Hasbro, Tesco, Verizon, and Qualcomm have tried to use hackathons to unleash creativity. Others, such as IBM, GM, Marriott, SAP, Toshiba, and GE, have invested heavily in design thinking. Still others such as Nordstrom, Bosch, GE, P&G, and Coca Cola have implemented lean start-up programs. Companies such as Lego, Samsung, Lilly, and Cisco have tried using open source innovation to spur new ideas.

Given the energy, time, and money spent on these innovation efforts, why haven’t the results been more impressive? As we illustrated in Chapter 3, to

manage disruption requires leaders to balance the tension between exploit- ing a core business that generates reliable, short-term results and exploring into new areas where results are uncertain, even if the long-term payoff may prove to be attractive.4 Too often organizations, faced with potential disrup- tion, focus on generating new ideas but struggle to convert these ideas into meaningful businesses. In almost every case of disruption (such as Block- buster, Sears, and Kodak) the firm falls victim to a business that they had tried unsuccessfully to build themselves. In these situations, there is often a plethora of ideas for how the firm might build the products, technologies, and business models that they see emerging in the new ecosystem. However, growing a new venture involves taking assets and capabilities (people and money) from existing profitable businesses and devoting them to more un- certain and often lower-margin new businesses that may even cannibalize existing ones. As we showed in Chapter 6, unless there is a clear strategy justifying the entrance into the new business, and unless senior management is prepared to protect these embryonic efforts, the tendency is for the mature business to either starve the new business or impose on it the performance standards of the mature business, an easy way to kill the new venture.

For these reasons, to be successful at ambidexterity requires firms to master ideation, incubation, and scaling. As we describe below, firms’ abil- ity to generate new ideas (ideation) has advanced greatly in the past twenty years, and many firms are rightly regarded as exemplars. A smaller number are also proficient at rigorously testing new business concepts, using meth- ods drawn mostly from the start-up arena (incubation). However, relatively few have successfully scaled new ventures to enable them to stay ahead of disruption (scaling). It is this last discipline that is critical to the success of new highly innovative corporate ventures. But it has received much less attention—and this is where ambidexterity becomes a key to success.

Ideation Generating new ideas is the first stage of successful ambidexterity. In most firms, research and development has responsibility for generating new ideas.
